question: A patient has a triangular fibrovascular growth on the nasal conjunctiva that appears to encroach onto the cornea. To distinguish pterygium from pseudopterygium, the MOST reliable bedside test is:

answers.text: Check for conjunctival follicles under the growth using a slit lamp

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Follicles are not relevant to distinguishing pterygium from pseudopterygium — this finding relates to inflammatory or infectious conjunctivitis.

answers.text: Attempt to pass a probe beneath the neck of the growth at the limbus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — the probe test. In pseudopterygium, the fold of conjunctiva is attached to the cornea only at its apex (often at a previous corneal injury site) and a probe can be passed freely beneath it at the limbus. A true pterygium is firmly adherent throughout its neck at the limbus and a probe cannot be passed.

answers.text: Measure intraocular pressure to assess for induced astigmatism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IOP measurement assesses glaucoma risk, not the nature of the growth. Corneal topography (not IOP) assesses pterygium-induced astigmatism.

answers.text: Apply fluorescein to check if the lesion stains, indicating corneal involvement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fluorescein staining assesses epithelial defects but does not differentiate pterygium from pseudopterygium.

overallFeedback.feedback: The probe test is the key clinical skill here: pass a probe under the neck of the lesion at the limbus. Pterygium: probe blocked (firmly adherent). Pseudopterygium: probe passes freely. Pseudopterygia are always associated with prior limbal injury.

Correct. The probe test is simple, fast, and definitive: free passage under the neck = pseudopterygium (secondary to previous injury/inflammation, not UV-driven); fixed adherence = true pterygium. This distinction changes surgical planning.
